transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Since my wife and I separated, I’ve felt this heavy, empty mood that I can’t shake, even when I’m at the library or around art. My niece noticed how much I've been struggling lately and persuaded me to come in and speak with someone.

I'm so sorry you're going through this difficult separation. To help me understand your situation better, how long ago did the separation happen, and how long have you been feeling this heavy, empty mood?

Thank you for your kind words. The separation became official and I moved into my own apartment about three months ago, which is exactly how long this heavy, empty mood has been hanging over me steadily. It just hasn't let up since I've been on my own.
Along with this heavy mood, have you noticed other changes such as trouble sleeping, a change in your appetite, or a constant lack of energy?

Yes, absolutely. Food mostly tastes like cardboard now so I just pick at a piece of toast, and at night I lie awake for hours looping over the separation before waking up at 4 AM unable to fall back asleep. My body also feels like it's moving through molasses, leaving me with so little energy that even shelving books at the library feels like a massive effort.
Have you also been experiencing feelings of worthlessness, or finding yourself blaming yourself excessively for the separation?

I definitely blame myself a lot for the separation, especially at night when I lie awake and my mind constantly loops over all the things I could have done differently. I wouldn't say I feel completely worthless overall as a person, but the regret and self-blame about my marriage ending is incredibly heavy.
During this difficult time, have you had any thoughts of wishing you were dead, or thoughts of hurting yourself?
No, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I just feel very empty, heavy, and exhausted, but I don't have any desire to hurt myself.
Have you ever experienced a period of feeling this down, empty, or exhausted at any other time in your life, or is this the first time you've felt this way?

Looking back, these dragging, low periods—and even some opposite, revved-up stretches—have actually been coming and going for many years throughout my life. While they aren't entirely new, they have become much more intense and noticeable over the past year as my marriage was falling apart.
During those "revved-up" periods, did you experience a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, or do things that were unusual or risky for you? How long did those periods typically last?

During those times, I'll only sleep about three or four hours a night but wake up feeling buzzing and energetic rather than tired. My mind jumps rapidly from topic to topic, and I throw myself into multiple projects at once, like planning workshops or reorganizing my whole apartment. These upbeat, high-energy periods usually last for just a few days at a time.
During those high-energy periods, do they ever last for four or more days in a row, and did family or friends notice a distinct change in your behavior?

Yes, those high-energy periods typically last for several days, usually anywhere from a few days to a week. Others definitely notice the shift; my coworkers and book-club friends commented on the marked change, and my adult niece even confronted me about how different I seemed and teased me for talking so fast without coming up for air.
Between these high-energy and low-energy phases, do you have periods lasting a couple of months or more where your mood feels completely normal and stable?

I'm not quite sure, to be honest, as I've never really thought about it that way. I always just chalked those shifts up to my personality or work stress, so I can't recall if there were long stretches where my mood was completely stable in between.

During those high-energy times, did your behavior ever lead to serious consequences, such as major financial problems, reckless decisions that harmed your relationships, or even needing to go to the hospital?

No, it never escalated to a major crisis like financial ruin, reckless danger, or needing to be hospitalized. While those periods made me overly intense, hyper-focused on projects, and sometimes irritable enough to snap at a coworker, they never caused any severe consequences like that.
Have you ever been diagnosed with a medical condition like thyroid issues, or were you using any substances or medications that could have triggered these high-energy periods?
No, I've never had any thyroid issues or other medical conditions that I know of. I also don't use any recreational substances or take any medications that could explain those high-energy times.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the criteria for Bipolar Affective Disorder (specifically Bipolar II disorder, though classified under the broader F31 code). He is currently experiencing a major depressive episode of 3 months' duration, characterized by depressed mood, insomnia, decreased appetite, psychomotor retardation, fatigue, and excessive guilt. He also reports a history of recurrent hypomanic episodes lasting several days to a week, characterized by a decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, increased goal-directed activity, and pressured speech. These high-energy episodes were noticeable to others but did not cause severe functional impairment, hospitalization, or psychotic features, and were not substance-induced, ruling out manic episodes and supporting a Bipolar II presentation.
